scope: Non-coal mining and critical minerals under the Ministry of Mines and the state mining departments: the ministers and Ministers of State with dates; the PSUs (NMDC, NMDC Steel, NALCO, Hindustan Copper, MOIL, KABIL, GSI); the MMDR Act 1957 and its 2015, 2021, 2023, 2025 and 2026 amendments and what each changed; the National Critical Mineral Mission (Jan 2025) and the central critical-mineral auction tranches including the twice-annulled Reasi lithium block; the Odisha 2020 iron-ore auction and the electoral bonds bought by Odisha miners; Niyamgiri bauxite; Goa's 2022 Bicholim award to Vedanta; the Adani MDO contract at Bailadila Deposit-13 and its termination; the Hindustan Zinc residual stake; NMDC Steel's stalled sale; and forest-land diversion for mining. The symmetry check runs three illegal-mining cases against three parties: Karnataka Lokayukta 2011 (BJP), Odisha Shah Commission/Supreme Court 2017 (BJD), Jharkhand ECI/ED v Hemant Soren 2022-24 (JMM). Deliberately left out: coal and lignite (Ministry of Coal, separate file), offshore mineral auction results, minor minerals, the block-by-block critical-mineral register already in research/raw/resources-minerals.json (whose facts are not re-asserted here unless re-opened), and the District Mineral Foundation corpus (no source could be opened; recorded as a gap).

claims.d: The 2015 amendment mandated auction for grant of mineral concessions, established the District Mineral Foundation and the National Mineral Exploration Trust, and stiffened penalties for illegal mining (ministry's own summary, 2023-08-02).

benefit.how: States receive auction premium on dispatched value on top of royalty; incumbents lost the first-come-first-served route (s.10A made pending applications ineligible).

claims.d: Passed LS 2021-03-19, RS 2021-03-22. No mine may be reserved for a particular end-use; existing captive mines may sell up to 50% of annual production in the open market after meeting their plant's needs (on an additional payment); the Centre may auction if a state fails to within a set time; statutory clearances transfer for the lease term; non-exclusive reconnaissance permits abolished.

benefit.how: Holders of captive iron-ore and coal leases (steel, cement, power groups) gained the right to sell half their output to the market, monetising ore previously locked to one plant; the class of beneficiary is every captive lessee, not a named firm. Boring explanation: the ministry's stated aim was to raise ore output and tax revenue.

claims.lab: critical minerals: 6 de-listed from atomic list; Centre auctions Part D; Exploration Licence
claims.d: Passed LS 2023-07-28, RS 2023-08-02. Removed lithium-, titanium-, beryllium-, niobium-, tantalum- and zirconium-bearing minerals from the 12 atomic minerals (opening them to private mining); empowered the Centre to exclusively auction MLs and CLs for 24 Part-D critical minerals (revenue to states) because states had auctioned only 19 of 107 blocks handed to them; created the Exploration Licence for deep-seated and critical minerals in a new Seventh Schedule to attract junior miners and FDI.

benefit.how: Private miners can now hold lithium, titanium, REE-adjacent and other formerly atomic-listed minerals; the first auction rounds were won mostly by large incumbents and PSUs (see c018-c022), not the junior explorers the amendment named as its target.

claims.lab: captive sale cap removed; critical minerals added to leases free; NMET→NMEDT 3%
claims.d: Introduced 2025-08-11, passed LS 2025-08-12, RS 2025-08-19. Removes the 50% cap on open-market sales from captive mines; lets lessees add critical and strategic minerals (lithium, graphite, nickel, cobalt, gold, silver named) to existing leases with no additional payment; enlarges lease areas for deep-seated minerals (>200 m) by up to 30% (CL) or 10% (ML); renames NMET the National Mineral Exploration and Development Trust with a 3% of royalty levy and power to fund development offshore and abroad; creates an authority to regulate mineral exchanges.

benefit.how: Every captive lessee (steel, cement, aluminium, power groups) may now sell 100% of surplus ore to the market; existing lessees can capture newly valuable critical minerals found in their leases without a fresh auction. Rivals: merchant miners lose the protection that captive ore stayed off the market; junior explorers lose blocks that would otherwise have been auctioned. Boring explanation: zero-waste mining and faster critical-mineral supply.

claims.lab: Centre regulates mineral-bearing lands; states barred from taxing mineral rights
claims.d: Introduced 2026-08-10, passed LS 2026-08-12, RS 2026-08-13. Empowers the Centre to regulate 'mineral bearing lands'; prohibits states from imposing any tax, cess or levy on mineral rights or mineral-bearing lands except on central conditions; and deems unpaid or unrecovered pre-commencement state levies invalid. Appears to answer the 2024 nine-judge Supreme Court ruling upholding states' power to tax mineral rights (that judgment was not opened here; see gaps).

benefit.how: Lessees escape state cesses on mineral rights and any retrospective demands for past levies; mineral-rich, mostly opposition- or regional-party-governed states (Odisha to 2024, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh) lose a revenue head. Karnataka has said it will challenge the Act. Boring explanation: uniform national levy regime after conflicting state cesses.

claims.d: The 2023 amendment is the legal basis for the central tranches launched from 2023-11-29; the ministry cites 'the Central Government's authority to grant mineral concessions for key minerals listed in Part D of the First Schedule'.

The premium is payable only on mineral dispatched, so a low bid on a block that may never produce is worth little. Vedanta group is the only Indian private group with operating base-metal mines and metallurgy, so its bidding across several blocks is the expected behaviour of the one qualified incumbent, not evidence of favour.

narratives.claim: Mining companies buy political access with electoral bonds and are rewarded with leases and clearances.
narratives.strongestCase: In Odisha, the ruling BJD's top ten bond donors were almost all miners, steel and cement makers (Essel 174.5, JSPL 100, Utkal 70, Rungta 50, Vedanta 40), and a local analyst told Forbes that no miner can operate without the state government's active cooperation. The Tribune found Rs 825 crore in bonds from firms with pending clearances or violations.
narratives.strongestCounter: The base rate is near-universal: virtually every large Odisha miner gave to the party in power, so the donation does not discriminate winners from losers. The two named pairings both cut the other way — Vedanta was fined by the NGT after buying bonds, and Essel's Bunder clearance was still pending five years on. The 2020 iron-ore blocks went to auction at >100% premiums, a mechanism that leaves little for a minister to give. No bond-to-award sequence with a dated decision was found.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A dated clearance, renewal or lease decision for a donor that departs from the treatment of a non-donor peer within months of a bond purchase; or ECI bond-matching data showing a donor's money moving to the party that controlled the decision at the decision date.

narratives.claim: The 2023-2026 MMDR amendments centralise control of mining at the expense of the states.
narratives.strongestCase: 2021: Centre may auction if a state does not. 2023: Centre exclusively auctions 24 critical minerals. 2025: NMET widened, captive cap removed centrally. 2026: Centre regulates 'mineral bearing lands', states barred from taxing mineral rights, past unpaid state levies deemed invalid; Karnataka has said it will go to the Supreme Court.
narratives.strongestCounter: Auction premium and royalty still accrue to the states even for central auctions; the ministry's stated reason (states auctioned 19 of 107 critical-mineral blocks) is a documented performance gap; a uniform levy regime is a defensible federal policy.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: The Supreme Court's ruling on Karnataka's challenge; data on how much state revenue the 2026 bar on levies removes.

narratives.claim: The Reasi lithium find makes India lithium-secure.
narratives.strongestCase: A 5.9-Mt inferred resource (GSI, Feb 2023 — figure not re-verified here) and a Rs 34,300-crore mission.
narratives.strongestCounter: The block has been offered twice and drawn no bid; it is explored only to G3; India's only awarded lithium block is Katghora in Chhattisgarh; KABIL's Argentine blocks are exploration-stage.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A G2 resource estimate and a successful re-auction with three qualified bidders.

narratives.claim: The Adani group is favoured in iron-ore mining.
narratives.strongestCase: AEL won the MDO contract for Bailadila Deposit-13 in 2018 from an NMDC-led JV.
narratives.strongestCounter: The mine never operated after tribal protests, and the PSU JV terminated the contract in August 2023 with unusually harsh language; the group's iron-ore footprint in this record is one lost contract. Its known mining strength is coal MDOs, outside this file.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: An iron-ore lease, MDO or port-linked ore contract awarded to the group on non-competitive terms; or an arbitration finding the termination wrongful.

narratives.claim: Vedanta is scooping up critical-mineral blocks cheaply.
narratives.strongestCase: Four of eight Tranche-IV blocks at the four lowest premiums (2.55-45%).
narratives.strongestCounter: Unproven tungsten/vanadium composite licences; three-qualified-bidder rule; premium payable only on dispatch; Vedanta is the only private group with the metallurgy to use them. Prior file's wider count (5 of 42 blocks in tranches IV-VII, ~12%) is a long-tail market, not capture.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Bid logs showing nominal competing bids on the Vedanta blocks; or the pattern repeating across tranches.

symmetryCheck: The lens 'official body finds illegal mining / self-dealing under this state government' was run on three iron-ore states under three parties. Karnataka (BJP, 2006-11): Lokayukta report 2011-07-27, Rs 16,085 crore loss, CM and ministers named, CM resigned. Odisha (BJD, 2000-2017): Shah Commission then CEC/Supreme Court 2017-08-02, Rs 17,576 crore notional illegal extraction, 102 of 187 leases in violation, 'inordinate delays' by the state in renewals, 100% recovery ordered. Jharkhand (JMM, 2019-24): ECI s.9A proceedings over a CM's self-allotted stone lease, opinion buried by the Governor; separate ED arrest and HC bail. The lens produced an adverse official record against every party it was pointed at, in each case authored by an independent body (Lokayukta, Supreme Court, ECI) rather than a rival party. Two conclusions: the method is not partisan, and 'illegal mining under party X' is a near-universal property of iron-ore states in the 2000s-2010s — non-discriminating by the project's own base-rate rule. The discriminating facts are the specific ones: who was named, what was recovered (Odisha: Rs 17,576 crore ordered; Karnataka: recovery outcome not verified here), and whether anyone was convicted (not established for any of the three in the opened sources). The one asymmetry worth recording: the Odisha record ends in a Supreme Court order enforcing recovery; the Karnataka and Jharkhand records end in unverified prosecutions and an unpublished ECI opinion.
